\chapter{The Heart}
\label{ch:ur-heart}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my heart in Urdu and trace dil to the same Indo-European root as Sanskrit hṛdaya and English heart, arriving by the Persian road instead of the Sanskrit one.}

Say merā dil, and trace it through Middle Persian and Proto-Iranian back to the same PIE *\'{k}ērd- that gives Sanskrit hṛdaya, English heart, Latin cor and Greek kardía — dil and hṛdaya split at the Indo-Iranian fork, not opposite lineages but the same root by two roads, echoing pūchhnā and porsīdan.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dil]{\ur{دل} — \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} Persian, and still a cousin of the English word}

\label{lesson:UR-C11-dil}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{منہ}}: its plain \textbf{\ur{ن}} marked a nasal vowel, and its possible tie to Greek \emph{mŷthos} was held loosely. Recall also \textbf{\ur{پوچھنا}}: one root, two roads into Urdu — inherited \emph{pūchhnā} and borrowed \emph{pursish}, cousins by two different paths. This chapter's single word runs that same two-roads shape one level deeper, on the body's most-named part.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{دل}} — \emph{dil} — \textbf{heart}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{دل۔}} — \emph{merā dil.} — \textquotedblleft{}my heart.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{دل}} is masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{دل}} is Persian — borrowed into Urdu from Middle Persian \emph{dil}, by the same road as \textbf{\ur{خدا}} back in Chapter 5. But unlike \textbf{\ur{خدا}}, whose Sanskrit side this book never named, \textbf{\ur{دل}} has one, and it is worth naming precisely.

Middle Persian \emph{dil} is itself \textbf{inherited}, not borrowed, within the Iranian branch of Indo-Iranian: from Proto-Iranian \textbf{*jārd}, from Proto-Indo-Iranian \textbf{*ȷ́\textsuperscript{h}\'{\={a}}rd}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*\'{k}ērd-}, \textquotedblleft{}heart.\textquotedblright{} That is the exact same root behind \textbf{Sanskrit} \emph{hṛdaya}, English \textbf{heart}, Latin \textbf{cor} (behind \emph{courage}, \emph{cordial}), and Greek \textbf{kardía} (behind \emph{cardiac}).

So \textbf{\ur{دل}} and Sanskrit's word for heart are not opposites, and they did not arrive by accident on the same idea. They are the \textbf{same PIE root}, split at the Indo-Iranian fork: one branch went east into Sanskrit and became \emph{hṛdaya}; the other went west into Iranian and became \emph{dil}, then travelled back into Urdu as a loan. Persian and Sanskrit both keep the family's heart-word — Urdu just happens to have taken the Iranian branch's copy.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dil} — heart; then \textbf{merā dil}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the four PIE cousins so far — \textbf{bhāī/brother, nāk/nose, āṅkh/eye, dil/heart}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{dil} $\leftarrow$ Middle Persian $\leftarrow$ Proto-Iranian $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*\'{k}ērd-} $\to$ Sanskrit \textbf{hṛdaya}
  \item \emph{Say it:} one root, two roads — Iranian and Indo-Aryan, the same shape as \textbf{pūchhnā}/\emph{pursish}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\ur{دل}}'s resemblance to Sanskrit \emph{hṛdaya} a coincidence, like \textbf{\ur{پسند}} and \emph{candēre}? (\textbf{No — both come from PIE \emph{\'{k}ērd-}, real cousins.}) Which branch of Indo-Iranian gave Urdu \textbf{\ur{دل}}, and which gave Sanskrit \textbf{hṛdaya}? (\textbf{Iranian; Indo-Aryan.}) Name three other English words from the same root as \textbf{\ur{دل}}. (\textbf{Heart, cardiac, courage} or \textbf{cordial}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AF\%D9\%84}{Wiktionary: \ur{دل}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
